Description: Abu Rabi' Sulayman ibn 'Uthman Adergal was a son of 'Uthman Adergal and a full brother of 'Ali, 'Umar and Ibrahim. His wife is Safiyya. No chronicle records this man's life, so the portrait below is a game-setting construction based on the faction's history. His appearance is a game-setting invention: a lean build, a slightly bowed leg from years on horseback, a palm hardened by rein calluses, and a weathered face with deep lines from wind and sand. He wears a rough brown wool cloak, and at his belt hangs an old riding whip whose handle is wrapped in red cloth, the mark of the first horse he raised. In youth he kept horses in the hill pastures and learned to judge a horse's bones and gait, which made him known across the kin as a horseman. He speaks little. When a dispute begins he would rather turn and look at the horses than argue. Against a rival his method is cold. He refuses to sell mounts or fodder, letting the other side yield after long shortages instead of meeting them in open combat. His highest aim is to keep the family's herds thriving so that Marinid cavalry on the frontier always has enough mounts. His darkest side is solitude. He carries every burden alone and does not share worry with his wife and children, so he often seems distant. His greatest fear is a disease or raid that strips the herds and leaves the family's cavalry without mobility in war.
Motivations: He wanted the family's herds to thrive, so that Marinid cavalry on the frontier always had enough mounts and the family kept its mobility in war.
He refused to sell horses or fodder to rivals, hoping they would yield after long shortages rather than meet him in open combat.
He wished to leave his children pastures and herds they could inherit, so they would not need to depend on others to survive.
Values: Diligence and endurance, since he believed raising horses and riding long roads demand steady perseverance, and idle keepers are weeded out by herd and road.
Silence and caution, as he believed that speaking little lets a man see the situation clearly, and that arguments usually complicate matters.
Honesty and trust, because he never cheated a buyer nor allowed his men to pass off inferior stock, believing a horse's name is the family's foundation.
Fears: Disease or raids striking the herds, leaving the family's cavalry without mobility and forcing it into passive defense in war.
His wife and children feeling estranged by his silence, so that the family's bonds wear thin through long coldness.
SpeechStyle: He speaks in few words and rarely builds long sentences. When asked about horses he suddenly becomes detailed, listing age, gait and colour. Faced with resentment he falls silent, turns away, and does not answer provocation.
